Introduction.What We Want: I want to slay monsters, quickly and with awesome combos. I want simple rules, but deep tactical thinking. I want freedom of choice and meaningful character progression, I want to feel like I am playing a medieval fantasy video game with my friends at the table. I want to run games for my friends, and tell my story at my own pace! I want no redundant rolls, few look-up tables, no Saving Throws or other elements that make the game slower. I want to farm mobs! I want to play like my generation of gamers wants to play! And this is why we made QuestGuard: a heroic tabletop role-playing game based both on slaying foes, and ever-growing characters. And if you want the same thing, you're in the right place. Keep on reading, stranger, and welcome to QuestGuard!

Welcome to QuestGuard.Text:
A role-playing game (RPG) is a game (either a video or at the table) where you control a hero, battle monsters and go on wonderous adventures and quests.
RPG's are one of the most common genres of video games, like Skyrim, Baldur's Gate, World of Warcraft, etc. To some extent, you can even consider games like League of Legends to be RPG's.

Imagine if instead of playing it on the computer, you played it with your friends at the table. And instead of being restricted to prewritten lines of dialogue, you can say whatever you want, to whomever you want, wherever you want. That's essentially a tabletop RPG! You can do anything you choose!
Of course, you need rules to play, like in a board game. So there are dice, maybe cards, abilities, and turn-taking between players.

And if you can literally say anything to any in-game character, no book or app could possibly contain the rules for every situation. Unless you're using a complex AI to run the world for you, we need something else. That's where the Quest Master comes in.
Welcome to QuestGuard.Quest Master: One of the players will play as a storyteller, called a Quest Master. They are the referee, judge and jury of the game. Generally, the Quest Master creates the world, narrates everything that happens, roleplays the characters you meet, controls the monsters, and designs the dungeons and quests you will explore. The job of the Quest Master is to make sure everyone has fun. The Quest Master is not the enemy, even though they play the monsters and villains. Ultimately, the Quest Master decides what is and isn't possible. If you say you want to “fly to the king, slay him, and teleport away,” you will need to respect the rules and get your Quest Master's approval to try that.
Welcome to QuestGuard.Trying Things: In Quest Guard, you can theoretically do anything. Or, at least, you can try. When you want to do something as a regular Hero (not the Quest Master), you usually need to roll dice to determine whether you succeed. This is called a “Check.” If you want to climb on top of a house, the Quest Master may ask you to roll a Check to see if you’re able to do it. Rolling a Check means rolling two regular cubic dice (called 2d6). If you roll high enough, you succeed. The Quest Master determines what total number you need to reach. Generally, rolling at least 10 means you succeed on a medium-difficulty Check. A difficult Check might require a 15 or higher. But hold on - the numbers you can roll range from 2 to 12. How could you ever roll a 15!? That's because you may get certain bonuses to your roll.

New QuestGuardians.Stats:
Each player's Hero is better or worse at certain things. If you're dexterous, you will get a bonus to the Check for climbing the house. Furthermore, if you're particularly good at climbing, you may get an additional on top of that!

your Hero has five main Stats that determine how good you are at different activities. These Stats are: Might (physical power and constitution), Instinct (agility and speed), Focus (knowledge and smarts), Presence (wisdom, willpower, and awareness), and Presence (social aptitude and confidence).

Each Stat ranges from -1 to +3, and they will grow over time as your Hero develops, in time.
If you have a +3 in Instinct, your Check to climb a house gains a +3 bonus. That means you don’t need to roll a 10 on the dice. You only need to roll a 7, which becomes a 10 after adding your bonus.

Suddenly, rolling high enough doesn’t seem so impossible anymore.
New QuestGuardians.How We Play:
The game is generally played as follows: the Quest Master describes a situation. Then, the players decide together how they want to react. Each player takes turns declaring their actions. After that, the Quest Master resolves what happens and presents a new situation. Rinse and repeat.

RPG stories are long. There are ways to lose, such as having all Heroes die. But there is no single way to win, and victory usually takes time. In fact, there may not even be a traditional “win” condition at all. Just like in a video game or TV series, success depends heavily on the Quest Master’s story.

Many adventures take multiple sessions to complete. In QuestGuard, we are committed to long journeys. You may meet with your friends over many days, picking up where you left off each time. That’s part of the magic—there is always more to discover.

You and your fellow players form a team. You are a band of adventurers, explorers, mercenaries, puzzle solvers, and sometimes even merchants or leaders.

Work together. Respect each other and the Quest Master. Leave no one behind!
New QuestGuardians.<aside>I Don't Really Get It...</aside>:
The best way to understand the game is to watch it being played. We recommend the “Force Grey: Lost City of Omu” series on YouTube, or any Critical Role campaign. Just make sure you start from the first episode.
Do note those series play Dungeons & Dragons, so while the rules may be different, the core vibe and feel are the same.

What You Need.2-4 Friends: Going out can be difficult, especially in a post-pandemic world. You can search for local Facebook or Discord gaming groups to find players. The most common tabletop RPG is Dungeons & Dragons (D&D), so many groups use “D&D” as shorthand for tabletop RPGs in general. Ask at local game stores or gaming cafés. If you live remotely, online play is more popular than ever. Join D&D or Looking For Group communities on Reddit, Facebook, or Discord and make a post. You'll find people quickly.

What You Need.Dice: You will need two six-sided dice for Checks, but a full RPG dice set is recommended. These include four-sided (d4), six-sided (d6), eight-sided (d8), ten-sided (d10), twelve-sided (d12), and twenty-sided (d20) dice. They are easy to find online or at game stores. If you play online, free digital dice rollers are widely available. Even Google has a built-in dice roller.

What You Need.The Rules: Congratulations! You already have them! This book contains the complete rules of the game and more. You can also find most of them online at https://questguardrpg.com, free of charge.

What You Need.Pen & Paper (or device): A notebook will be your best friend in writing notes, keeping track of your quest journal, and, most importantly, tracking your Hero's powers. Luckily, if you hate writing by hand, we have online tools on our website to help you keep track of your Hero. More on that later!

What You Need.Other: Many RPG groups use miniature figures, terrain, maps, etc. The fun part in tabletop RPG's is you can make your own board, on a square grid each representing one meter, and figurines or tokens to represent each character. While you don't necessarily require a grid and miniatures, we recommend using something (anything) to represent each character on the battlefield. Of course, if you're playing online, all of that will be taken care of for you!

New QuestGuardians.<aside>Is There a Tutorial?</aside>: Yes! Simply search “how to play QuestGuard” on YouTube to find dedicated video tutorials that walk you through everything step by step.

What is QuestGuard?.Text:
QuestGuard is a gamified tactical tabletop roleplaying game for the younger generation, who are more used to video games and board games, and want a fast, rules-light, combat-focused alternative to the mainstream and older systems: it’s the opposite of old-school!

While playing QuestGuard, you will find more “gamified” elements, both for the players and for the Quest Master. There is an emphasis on build variety, combos, and rules to help Quest Masters have an easier time, and depth through interactions, not complexity.

We created QuestGuard out of love for tabletop roleplaying, to fit our needs and, most importantly, to fit with how the current generation actually plays combat RPGs.

If you’ve played Dungeons & Dragons or Pathfinder, you will find QuestGuard very easy to pick up!
What is QuestGuard?.Is this a spin-off?: Nope! QuestGuard is its own game, completely separate from other traditional fantasy roleplaying games!
What is QuestGuard?.What to expect?:
QuestGuard is systems-light: there is no roll to hit, there are hardly any tables, no concentration, no spell components or spell slot levels, no opportunity attacks, no saving Checks in combat (crowd control/status effect is direct and fair).
There are no long or short rests, as the Quest Master has better control over the pacing through the Adventure and Enemy Worthiness system.
There is are proficiency systems, no stat-to-skill lists, damage reduction from defenses, success degrees, diminishing returns on actions, and the list keeps on going!

Character abilities are gamified for gameplay rather than realism, to be able to do things such as creating gold or magic items out of thin air or farming enemies. Characters can respec between Adventures, all monsters are tactical and change how you must approach combat, and this is just the tip of the iceberg!

Also, QuestGuard a 2d6 game as opposed to d20, and follows a 3-Action-Point system.
What is QuestGuard?.How To Start?:
You're in the right place! You can create a character, quickly and without hassle, using our Hero Creator, going to Create Hero in the website menu. It will take you through everything you need!
Also, our website https://questguardrpg.com features a “Play With Us!” button. Once clicked, it will redirect you to our Discord group, where we regularly host campaigns and one-shot adventures for new and old players alike!

Feel free to say hi and show your Hero!

/Why QuestGuard?.Being a Quest Master is easy: uestGuard is made to be cool for players, and easy and fun for the Quest Master (the game master). Through rules such as the Adventure, Worthiness, Skills, Quirks, etc, you will find running Quest Guard both enjoyable and easy to manage.
/Why QuestGuard?.Always online: All the resources are always online. As such, there are frequent patches, balance improvements, content updates, and much, much more!

/Dice.Text: QuestGuard is a 2d6 system. Whenever you roll a Check, you roll 2 6-sided dice and add any modifiers to it. Rolling evens (1-1, 2-2, 3-3, and so on) means getting Plot Points! If it was a success, you gain a Plot Point. Otherwise, the Quest Master gains a Plot Point. Spend Plot Points to introduce Actually facts to the current situation, whether you’re a Quest Master or a player. Here are some examples: “Actually, the shopkeep did leave a window open…” “Actually, there is a chandelier I could swing on…” “Actually, since your Hero has Claustrophobia, they are afraid to take this short route.”
/Dice.Which dice are used: In QuestGuard, we use the standard polyhedral dice: d4, d6, d8, d10, d12 and d20 (although the d20 is rarely used). Hint: we actually also use d2 and sometimes troll players with a d14 (but it's only sometimes, we promise!)
/Dice..Combat Dice:
In combat, there is no rolling to hit. Whenever you attack, you roll for Damage directly - most of the time, what you see is what you get. If you rolled a total of 14 on 3d6, you deal 14 Damage.

By default, there are no critical strikes, but some weapons and Abilities can trigger bonus effects based on the rolls. If it can, it is neatly mentioned in its text box.

{Item(Bow)}

Most of the time, you will deal and take Damage. Be prepared

/Hero.Hero Creation:
Like in most RPG’s, a Player Character needs a character sheet. Normally, we do it online, on the website, with a dedicated Hero builder.
You can find it on the website at https://questguardrpg.com under Create Hero.

Of course, if you want to do it on paper, you’re free to do so, and you can download the Hero Sheet under Game, Downloads, Hero Sheet (PDF, PNG, or PSD).

The proper process for crating a Hero is explained in-depth at the Hero Creation chapter, after this chapter.
/Hero.What Makes a Hero Different:
A Hero is made up of a Race plus a Class. Each of these has a ton of customization options.

Each Race is different, and you can customize it with 2 Racial Features! Every Level, you get a choice of one out of 3 or more Talents to pick from your Class. Talents are powerful Abilities that shape how your Character plays and fights.

Don’t be afraid to try strange combinations! Heroes Characters can freely “respec” between missions, changing all Talent choices and learned Abilities
/Hero.Progression:
There are 10 Levels Players can progress through with their Characters.

Levels are packed with interesting options. Every Level unlocks new Abilities, and every Adventure ends with players getting Quirks!

The recommended way to Level-Up is through milestones or checkpoints set by the Quest Master. If using the Experience system, however, going from Level 1 to Level 10 should not take an eternity, either. QuestGuard intends campaigns to play out spanning a few months at most, but it’s all up to you and your group.
/Hero.Stats: There are 4 Main Stats in QuestGuard: Might, Instinct, Focus, and Presence. The Stat is directly the “modifier”. In combat, each Stat affects an aspect of your character.
Text: Focus affects Initiative (+0.5 / point), and you get +1 Action Point on your first Turn per 1 Initiative.
/Hero.<aside>Quick Note</aside>: You can’t actualy have Movement and Initiative in fractions! Round it down: 1.5 is the same as 1, -0.5 is the same as -1.
/Hero.Text2: All Stats also contribute to Checks.

Plus, don’t worry, you get +1 in any Stat every Level!
/Hero./Skills & Substats:
There isn't a predetermined list of Skills on your Hero Sheet. 

When you want to do something, the Quest Master will simply call out for a “Might Check” or a Presence Check”, for example (2d6).

However, each Hero will have non-combat Skills they can add themselves to the Roll if appropriate.
Each Skill you have explicitly has a bonus (e.g. +3 in Persuasion, +1 in Monstrology, -2 in Control Emotions, etc).

The Quest Master might call for a Presence Roll to ask a quest giver for more reward money, and, if you have a Skill that fits, you can say “I have a +2 in Convincing, can I add it to the roll?”, to which the Quest Master might say yes or no, depending on the situation.

Feel free to invent your own Skills, but you can find a list of recommendations on the website.

The main sense, though, are separate from eachother (e.g. + in Smelling, Sight, Hearing, etc).
/Hero..Abilities:
Almost everything you get in this game is an Ability. Skills, spells, attacks, moves, Feats, Talents, even weapons and armor!

An Ability is simply a rectangle with a clearly defined text, a little colorful icon and tags to help you identify its properties, such as the costs of using it, how often you can use it, the range, etc.

{Spell(Rime Shackles)}

Most of the time, the only thing you need to use an Ability is your hands. No need for materials, a focus, spoken words, etc.
/Hero.<aside>Nifty website trick</aside>:
On the website, click on the little document icon on the bottom-right of an Ability to copy it to your clipboard. You can then paste it in a Word document, in Paint, Discord, etc.
Your Hero in the Hero Creator online will also display a list of all your Abilities, and you can even use the Ability Sheet Maker tool on the website! TODO add more details.

/Combat.Text:
Combat usually happens on a map, preferably on a grid, and distances are measured in meters. In game, 1 meter is the equivlent of 1 space or 5 feet. 

Turn order is clockwise around the table, with monsters somewhere in-between players.
/Combat..Combo:
Many Abilities and weapons “apply a Combo”.
Many Abilities and weapons trigger an extra effect if the target had a Combo! Then the Combo is removed.

Anyone can trigger anyone’s combo. Go make some combos with your team!
/Combat.Mana:
The resource used to cast more powerful Abilities is called Mana. Most Classes use Mana.

You have a number of Mana Points you can use on Abilities.
If you have 5 Mana Points and an Ability requires 2 Mana, you spend 2 Mana and use the Ability. Then, you are left with 3 Mana.

Usually, Mana regenerates in the downtime between Adventures.
/Combat.Resting & regeneration:
There are no rests like short rests or long rests.

You regenerate Health equal to your Health Regen after every Combat. Your Health Regen is defined by your Race.
You regenerate all resources (Health, Mana, Cooldowns, etc) at the end of every Adventure.
/Combat.Adventures:
An Adventure is a time period defined by the Quest Master. It could be a full dungeon, a play session, completing a quest, etc.

An Adventure that makes will have you use everything in your will to survive you will typically contain 3 medium-difficulty combat.

/Important Concepts.Text: So far so good? Let’s discuss some extra things you should know, to get you up to speed.
/Important Concepts.Turn Order:
Players may take Turns clockwise (or counter-clockwise) around the table, starting from any player they choose.
Monsters have a stat called Setback that tells them after how many players they can take their Turn.
/Important Concepts.Initiative:
Your Initiative does not affect Turn order, but tells you how many extra Action Points you get on your first Turn in Combat.

Monsters usually don’t have Initiative.
/Important Concepts.Quirks:
At the end of every Adventure, each Player Character gets a Quirk, be it positive or negative, based on their performance. These can be phobias, extra Health from being healthy, etc.

We’re still testing out Quirks, so the system is not entirely nailed down, but it works!
/Important Concepts.Balance:
The game is balanced mathematically with tables and calculations, so that you may pick any Class and Race combination and have no disadvantage over other players.
Naturally, not everything is perfect, and balance is subject to change. TODO maybe remove this section.
/Important Concepts.Tools: The website is full of useful tools, such as the Character Creator, Ability Sheet Maker, etc. Make sure you explore and use them!
/Important Concepts.Premium Content:
There are menus and pages with a {Premium} icon.
This represents Premium Content that will be available only via purchasing it.
The basic rules and content (Basic Set) is fully available and always free, and the game is fully playable with the Basic Set. At the time of writing this book, the Core Set is the first expansion of the game, and requires purchasing.

Get Started.How Do I Start?:
You’re already in it!
You can create a character, quickly and without hassle, using our Hero Creator, going to Create Hero in the website menu. It will take you through everything you need!
Also, our website https://questguardrpg.com features a “Play With Us!” button. Once clicked, it will redirect you to our Discord group, where we regularly host campaigns and one-shot adventures for new and old players alike!

Feel free to say hi and show your Hero!
Get Started.What To Expect?: In QuestGuard you will find more “gamified” elements, both for the heroes and for the Quest Master. The game plays somewhat like a board game, but one in which you have more freedom of choice. Character abilities are gamified for gameplay rather than realism, to be able to do things such as creating gold or magic items out of thin air or farming enemies. Characters can respec between Adventures, all monsters are tactical and change how you must approach combat, and this is the tip of the iceberg! There is some math involved, but most often, what you roll on the dice is what you get. There will be halving and doubling of numbers involved, some simple addition, and rarely subtraction. If long tables, lists and big boxes of rules text scare you, that's perfect! We avoid that in QuestGuard as much as possible.
Get Started.Non-Combat: While QuestGuard heavily focuses on battling enemies, there are 2 different types of gameplay: in-combat and non-combat. While not in combat, ther game focuses on the narrative aspect and interaction with the adventure constructed by the Quest Master. Traveling is abstract, there are more intricate descriptions, and time in-game passes abstractly, like in a book or movie. You may jump from scene to scene, from day to day, from moment to moment, doing things as you see fit. It's more abstract than palpable.
Get Started.Combat: When combat begins, the pace shifts. Heroes and monsters will take turns, like in a board game, to try to defeat eachother. We use specific rules for attacking, casting spells, being hit, etc. It's more palpable than abstract. For example, during Combat, on your Turn, you have 3 Action Points each Turn that you can spend to do things, like move, attack, etc. You could spend 1 Action Point to move, then 1 Action Point to attack with a shortsword, then your last Action Point can be spent to cast a Spell. There's a specific section for Combat later on.

Playing the Game.Text: Unlike board games and video games, QuestGuard requires you to use your imagination to create a so-called "theater of the mind". The Quest Master will do their best to immerse you in the story with lush descriptions of environments and characters in the story, and they may even show you reference images and music for what things look, sound, and feel like. Do you feel it? The atmosphere, the tension? Let yourself speak in the voice of your hero, and imagine, if for one second, that the people you're speaking to are the Heroes and story characters you're interacting with.
Playing the Game.Example of Play: Quest Master David: You finally made it to the meeting point. Your contact, Varis, sits across from your, warming his hands at the campfire crackling softly in the forest clearing. "You're late" he mutters. Arin the Knight: I say boldly "We had company on the road. But nothing has stopped us so far." Quest Master David: Varis replies "Curious..." Lira the Mage: That's all he says? Something feels wrong. Can I check if there's anything suspicious about him? Quest Master David: Sure. Make a Presence roll. You're going to need at least 10. Lira the Mage: Here goes... 2d6... that's a 9. If I add my +2 Presence, that's an 11! Quest Master David: Success! His face is right. His voice is right. But as the fire flares… his shadow stays perfectly still. Arin the Knight: I approach lighty and ask him "Can you raise your hand for me?" Quest Master David: He looks surprised, but raises his hand. You notice his shadows hasn't moved. Lira the Mage: That's not a human! It's an ambush! Quest Master David: Varis reveals his sharp fangs as he grins, and quickly lunges at you! Prepare for battle!
Playing the Game.For Heroes:
If you're set on being a protagonist in the story, here's what you need to do: talk to your Quest Master to see what kind of adventure you'll be playing. Then, you and your friends (except Quest Master) each creates a Hero, so that your team is diverse and ready to face any obstacle!

Remember: while it's a Hero's journey to follow the main story, you might have your own story and character arc!
It all depends on what kind of adventure you play, and what kind of Quest Master you have.
Playing the Game.For Quest Masters:
If you like to tell intricate stories, create epic worlds, and like to entertain others, you should definitely be the Quest Master! You're the narrator, the referee, and the HR department of your group.

Think of a story you want to tell. If you like vampires (like our friend Varis earlier), then make an adventure about vampires. If you like , make an adventure about dragons. If you like the Lord of the Rings, no one is stopping you from recreating it with your friends, or even expand on it by holding adventures in the that universe!

However, note that Heroes will always choose a different course of actions. Let them! Let them keep the Ring and face Sauron in face-to-face combat! You just never know what the Heroes will do and how the story will progress. Let them try!

But a small piece of advice: if you've never done this before, start small. Start with a short adventure around a village, or a journey through the mountains for an artefact. If it works out, keep expanding the story to keep the players engaged.

There is a Quest Master guide at the second half of the book, at page TODO. You can read it for guidelines and tips from the very best of game masters.

Hero.Text:
Before setting out on your quests, you need a Hero to play as. Talk to your fellow Quest Master and players about what kind of group you want to be, and decide what role each of you should fill.
A good party contains both close-range Heroes and artillery Heroes, one or more spellcasters and support or healer role. Of course, nothing is stopping you from being a full 5-people group of wizards!
Hero.Character's Concept:
After deciding what role you want to fill, you should determine your broader concept for a Hero. Are you an orc barbarian seeking to avenge his tribe? An elf sorceress seeking a cure for her magical curse? Or a human farmer who was forced out of his town and into the greater world.
What is your narrative, what is your ancestry, and what is your specialization?
What are you good and bad at? What are you afraid of and what do you like? What is your relationship to your other party members? Did you know eachother before setting out, or did you meet in a tavern? Are any of the two of your brothers, lovers, or enemies?
And most importantly, what is your name?

What Makes a Hero.Text: Each Hero must pick a Race, a Class, and some starting equipment. All of these will be written on your Hero Sheet -- a piece of paper (or web page) that contains all the information about your Hero. Listed here are the basics of each. There are separate chapters for the Race and Class. Follow them, in order.
What Makes a Hero.A. Hero Sheet: You will need a place to keep track of all your Hero's abilities and aptitudes. You can either use a sheet of paper that you can print and fill in the fields, or use the online My Character tracker.
What Makes a Hero.B. Race: Your Race is your species, and each species has plenty of different ancestries to pick from. Your Race determines not just your roleplay and story opportunities, but also your physical and mental capabilities. Giants are usually larger and stronger than Littlefolk. But that's not to say you can't have a Littlefolk who is stronger than a Giant! You will find all the options summarized in the next pages.
What Makes a Hero.C. Class: Your Class is your combat archetype. Examples of Classes are Warrior, Wizard, Rogue and Hunter, but there are plenty of Classes to pick from, each with hundreds of possible ways to play!
What Makes a Hero.D. Equipment: Every Hero needs solid armor, a trusty blade or a mage's robe if that's your type. You'll have a budget of 1000 Gold to spend to buy your starting equipment.

Hero.Let's Go!: Following, you will find a reference with all core Races and Classes in QuestGuard. Pick a combination of 2 that you like, without worrying about the nitty-gritty, then we'll start filling in that character sheet! If you are completely new to this type of game, we recommend sticking to easy Races and Classes.

Races Reference.Bertle: Bertles are animal people. Big, small, scaly or furry, they come in all shapes and sizes!
Races Reference.Dragon: Dragons scare mortals. Hero Dragons may be large and fierce, or have humanoid forms.
Races Reference.Dwarf: Dwarves are short but stout. They are the miners, builders and vikings of fantasy.
Races Reference.Elf: Elves have a very wide range of genes. High Elves, Wood Elves, Dark Elves, Snow Elves...
Races Reference.Giant: Giant is a term encompassing large creatures, like Orcs, Ettings, Ogres, and other.
Races Reference.Human: Humans are everywhere, with a wide array of skills.
Races Reference.Hollow: Hollows are the accursed of the universe, the Vampires, Werewolves and the Undead.
Races Reference.Littlefolk: Littlefolk are the Gnomes, Goblins, Gremlins, Leprechauns... oh, the Leprechauns...

Artificer.Text: Inventors who trade their Presence for advancement. They brew potions, build devices, and may graft metal or mutations onto themselves and allies. Some seek perfection through metal, others embrace humanity. As they level, their choices permanently reshape who they are, getting closer that ideal form.

Cleric.Text: Wielders of light and shadow, whose actions trigger Awe, damaging foes or Healing allies. As they level, their Awe becomes stronger but more focused on their faith in the light or the dark.They can fill any role, nd Some of their blessings become permanent.

Druid.Text: Nature-bound spellcasters whose magic changes with the environment. Each spell gains altered or enhanced effects based on terrain, weather, or elemental presence. Shapeshifting is optional, but specialists can build entirely around adaptive beast forms.

Hunter.Text: Tacticians who fight through customized animal companions. They rely on positioning, tracking, and pet synergy rather than spellcasting. Many talents enhance or modify their pets instead of themselves, and Beastmasters can command two permanent companions.

Knight.Text: Armored combo fighters who chain abilities together. Each attack improves the next, rewarding sequencing and planning. Their chosen Creed defines their style, such as the Creed of the Rose, Dragon, or Crown, and they employ squires, mounts, banners, or siege tools to shape the battlefield.

Rogue.Text: High-burst assassins and precision thieves. They don’t use mana — instead, every talent is a powerful Major Talent, built for decisive plays. They specialize in single-target elimination and economic manipulation, turning cunning into lethal advantage.

Shaman.Text: Spirit-channelers whose spells can echo to cast twice through spiritual resonance. They guide allies towards enlightenment and inner clarity, empowering their team through shared spiritual balance and unpredictable duplication.

Sorcerer.Text: Uncontrollable magic gamblers. Each turn, they roll a customizable 1d10, triggering unique effects based on the result. Players define what each number does, shaping their own chaos engine while riding unpredictable surges of power.

Swashbuckler.Text: Charming duelists and fearless fencers who live for spectacle. They leap, taunt, and fish for critical strikes, chaining them into deadly flourishes. Built for high noon standoffs, duel-to-the-death showdowns, and swinging on chandeliers in pursuit of glory.

Warlock.Text: Combatants who gain Evoke Points during battle and spend them on devastating effects. Though often seen as dark spellcasters, Warlocks are highly versatile, able to tank, Heal, wield weapons, or dominate with magic depending on their source of magic.

Warrior.Text: Combat generalists who choose a personal War Craft to define their style. They use mana to wield wide tactical options, and can even borrow Fire or Frost spells as physical techniques and martial effects. Built for flexibility, they can deal damage, protect allies, or even Heal to fill hybrid roles.

Wizard.Text: Elemental specialists with the largest mana pools and the widest spell access. They focus on Fire, Frost, Shock, or pure arcane magic. The longer combat lasts, the stronger they become, scaling steadily into overwhelming power.

Hero Sheet.Which One To Get: You can either download and print a Hero Sheet from the website, navigating to the Game tab and clicking on Hero Sheet under the Downloads section. You can print it and fill it in with a pen. If you prefer to do it digitally, there's also a form-fillable PDF version, under the same Downloads section. You can open it on a device with an app like Adobe Acrobat or Google Chrome, fill in the forms, and save it somewhere safe. Finally, if you want to go full digital and store your character in the cloud, you can log in with a Google account on the website and click on Create Hero. There you can simply follow the tabs one by one, going through each choice, then hit Save. Simply follow the guidelines and tips displayed. The process for using the Create Hero app may be slightly different, depending on when you're reading this. There are also a few pregenerated Heroes you can use as an example, to help you through your Hero creation.
Hero Sheet.Names:
Start by filling in the name of your Hero, and your chosen Race and Class. On the right side (WIP) of the sheet, you will find a blank space where you can either draw or stick an image of what your Hero looks like. If you prefer writing, you can jot down how your character looks, what aura they give, and their overall personality.
You can write about their goals, backstory, fears, and wants. And feel free to personalize the rest of your character sheet's empty space with drawing, writing or whatever will make it feel more homely.

Level.Text:
Each Hero's advancement in their adventure is noted by their Level. A Hero usually starts at Level 1 and can grow stronger and more keen up until Level 10, which is the maximum Level.
Some Quest Masters opt to start their story with Heroes already more advanced, and at higher Levels! If so, then simply start at Level 1, and then follow the steps detailed in the Leveling Up chapter, on page TODO.
Level.+Experience:
A Hero Levels up when they gain enough experience through adventuring. The Quest Master may award Experience Points to Heroes who complete quests, slay enemies, engage in meaningful roleplay, solve problems and puzzles, etc.
Every Hero starts with 0 Experience Points (XP).

To Level Up, you need an extra number of XP equal to 100 × your Level. Thus, when you are Level 1, you need 100 XP to reach Level 2. Then you need another 200 XP to reach Level 3, then another 300 XP to reach Level 4, and so on.

Some Quest Masters opt out of Experience entirely, and award Levels directly after reaching certain milestones in the story. If you're a beginner Quest Master, this is the recommended approach to managing your players' Heroes' Levels.

Stats.Text: There are 4 Stats in QuestGuard, and these reflect your aptitudes: Might ({MightCalculation}), Instinct (speed and agility), Focus (knowledge and magic prowess), Presence (the 5 senses and willpower), and Presence (social game and initiative).

Fill in the 5 Stats.Text: On your Hero sheet, you have 5 boxes on the left (WIP), each corresponding to one of the 5 Stats. You need to fill these boxes with the numbers -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, in any order you like. For example, if your Hero is very intelligent but quite frail, you can have 3 in Focus and -1 in Might.
Fill in the 5 Stats.Restrictions: However, note that some Races will impose some restrictions on the way you distribute your Stats, namely Bertle, Giant, and Hollow. I recommend starting with a Race that is tagged as Easy on the Race quick-reference page.

Stats.What Stats Do: Whenever you roll a Check (2d6), you will add your appropriate Stat to that Check. For example, if the Quest Master wants you to make a Presence Check, you will roll 2d6 and add your Presence to that roll (yes, even if your Presence is -1)!

What Each Stat Does.Might: Increases your maximum Health (each Might increases your Max Health by 3).

What Each Stat Does.Instinct: Increases your Movement Speed (each Instinct increases your Movement Speed by 0.5 meters).

What Each Stat Does.Focus: Increases the number of Spells and Abilities you can have (each Focus allows you to pick an extra Talent, explained later).

What Each Stat Does.Presence: Increases your Health Regen after combats (each Presence increases your Health Regen by 2).
Increases the number of Actions you can take on the first Turn each combat (each Presence increases your Initiative by 0.5).

Stats.Skills: Skills are non-combat activities that your Hero is better at. These are activities like Climbing, Jumping, Smelling, Sight, Magic, etc. You can invent your own skills, or take a look at the skill ideas list for inspiration. Each Skill you have has a number, which is the bonus you get when you make a Check for that specific activity. For example, if you want to jump over a cliff, and you have 3 Dexterity and +2 in Jumping, you will roll a total of 2d6 + 5. How to get Skills: You have a number of Skill Points equal to 2 + your Intelligence. You can spend each Skill Point to add +1 to a Skill, be it a new one or one your already have. For example, if you have 1 Intelligence, you have a total of 3 Skill Points, which you can distribute as: +1 Magic, +2 Listening. Or you could go full in on +3 Magic, or just have +1 in 3 different Skills, like +1 Magic, +1 Occultism, +1 Sight.
Stats.<aside>Skills in Combat & limits</aside>: Note that Skills only affect Checks. Even if you have +1 in Running, you do not gain +1 Movement Speed, but might be better in situations where running is required. Also, none of your Skills can exceed your highest Stat. If it does, the bonus is limited to your highest Stat.

Race & Combat Attributes.Text: Next up, we will complete the Hero Sheet with everything the Race gives you, plus the Combat Attributes on your Hero Sheet. You will want to put a bookmark on this page and the Race page, because you will need to flip between them. First, flip to your Race's page (or navigate online on the website to your Race's web page). The Races section of the book starts at page (WIP).

Combat Attributes.Text: Near the 5 Stats, on the center of the page (WIP), you will find the 4 Combat Attributes: Max Health, Health Regen, Movement Speed, and Initiative. Some of these are self explainatory, but we will go one by one and fill them in. Your chosen Race will determine your Max Health and Health Regen, so we will start with those.
Combat Attributes.Max Health: Max Health (or HP) determines how many hits you can take in battle before you go down. If you have 10 Health and take a hit for 6 Health, you will be left with 4 Health. Fill In: Check your Race's page. Under Race Features, there's a box (WIP) for Max Health. Calculate your Max Health based on what it says in that box. This calculation is always a flat number (different for each Race), plus your Might × 3.
Combat Attributes.Health Regen: Health Regen (HR) determines how much HP you recover after each fight. If you have 4 Health left out of 10, and your Health Regen is 5, you will be left with 9 Health after the combat is finished. Fill In: Check your Race's page. Under Race Features, there's a box (WIP) for Health Regen. Calculate your Health Regen based on what it says in that box. This calculation is always a flat number (different for each Race), plus your Presence × 2.
Combat Attributes.Movement Speed: When you use 1 Action Point to move (out of the 3 you have per Turn), you can move a number of meters, determined by your Movement Speed. If you have 5 Movement Speed and decide to spend 1 Action Point to move, you can move up to 5 meters. Fill In: Your Movement Speed is 4, plus 0.5 for each Instinct you have, but the result is always rounded down. For example, if your Instinct is 1, then your Movement Speed is 4.5 meters. Therefore, you can move 4 meters.
Combat Attributes.Initiative: On your first Turn each Combat, you gain extra Action Points based on your Initiative! The higher your Initiative, the more explosive your Combats will be. Fill In: 0.5 for each Presence you have. For example, if you have 2 Presence, your Initiative is 1, and you get 1 extra Action Point at the start of each Combat. Therefore, you will start Combats with 4 Action points instead of 3! Note that fractions (e.g. 1.5) are rounded down. So even if your Initiative is 1.5, you still only get +1 Action Point (no such thing as half-action points).
Combat Attributes.Done!: That was the hard math part! Next, let's continue with something easier and with more freedom.

Languages and Other.Text: The number of languages your Hero knows is based on Focus, but each Race may give you different base languages. Check your Race's Languages section, at Race Features. By default, everybody speaks Common (English). No 2 stories and adventures are the same, therefore there isn't a set-in-stone set of languages to pick from. This is where you should ask your Quest Master what languages are present in your story. Perhaps there is no Elvish, or goblins speak Italian. Decide on your langauges together with your Quest Master.

Abilities.Text: You are now about to get your first Abilities! An Ability is a power, which can be either active (requiring manual activation) or passive (always there in the background, or one-time-use). From this point on, almost everything in the game is an Ability: spells, weapons, armor, Talents, Feats, and act as the powers your Hero has. You can recognize an Ability by seeing that it looks like a playing card (in the book). On the website, an Ability looks like a box with a little icon on the left, and text down below. Each Ability clearly displays what it does, and has a set of tags that tell your how many Action Points it uses (if any), its duration, its cost, any specific requirements, etc. (TODO: add icons here and example)
Abilities.<aside>No Other Requirements!</aside>: There are truly no other requirements for using an Ability, whether it's a Spell or not! No material components, no wands or arcane foci, no need for empty hands, etc. The only requirements are paying the cost and spending the Action Points.
Abilities.Organizing Abilities: It's difficult to manually write by hand all your Abilities, so there are several tools to organize your Abilities, most of them online. Pick one of the following options to track your Abilities. We recommend the first option with the printed cards. Printed Cards: Make a list of all your Abilities that you get (just the names). When you finish creating your Hero, go to the website at Game, Abilities, and click on Print Abilities (WIP). Then input by name all Abilities you have and the website will give you some A4 (or letterbox WIP) paper images that you can download, print, and cut. You will always have these Ability cards at hand. Online Tracker: Make a list of all your Abilities that you get (just the names). Login on the website, then go to Game, Abilities, and click on Ability Sheet Maker (WIP). Add all your Abilities there, input the name of your Hero and hit save. From now on, you can go to that page and always see all Abilities you have. Hero Creator: If you opted to use the Hero Creator on the website, things are much easier. You can simply hit Select on Abilities as you come accross them, and they will appear under the My Character tab, at the bottom of the page (scroll down). Write By Hand: If you prefer the old-school way of doing things, you can simply write the Abilities down on a sheet of paper, use a spreadsheer, or a Word document, etc. It's all up to you!

Race Abilities.Text: On your Race's page, check the Starting Abilities section (WIP). Each Race gives you some Abilities that you start with. For example, the easiest ones are probably for the Dwarf. Dwarves only get 1 Starting Ability called Stouthearten. Merely having this Ability allows your Character to wear 2 sets of armor simultaneously! Write that down on your Character Sheet, on the bottom-right (WIP).

Race Talent Abilities.Text: Here is where your Hero becomes different from other Heroes of the same Race. Each Race gets to pick 2 different Abilities from the Race Talents (WIP) section. Read them carefully, see what you like, and write them to your Abilities. When you're done, come back to this page and we will get started with the Class!

That's All.Text: That's all for the Race! But the real skillset of your Hero comes from your Class, which will determine your fighting capabilities and your approach to encounters!

Class.Text:
Your Class is what gives life to your Hero, it is what makes it unique and what influences your play style the most. It is akin to your job: a Warrior is a master of weapons and physical combat, a Rogue is a trickster with thieving skills and assassination expertise, a Wizard is the master of pyromancy, arcanism, and the elements. Feel free to choose whichever you think suits your playstyle better. There are tons of Classes available in QuestGuard in this book.
If you haven't decided on a Class yet, take a look at them on the Class reference sheet and go by the gut feeling for your first Hero, though some of the Classes are easier to play than other. I recommend picking an easy Class that fits youts Hero fantasy.
Class.Class Abilities: Your Class gives you access to two or three starting Abilities. These are the core of your Hero's fighting style. Take note of them, or, if you're using the Hero Creator online, they were already added to your Hero Sheet when you selected the Class. If you find anything confusing, each Ability has a more detailed explanation either in the subtext, or on the Class's page.

Mana.Text: Many Classes in the game use a system of points called Mana Points. It is the main resource you will use for casting Spells and using Abilities. For instance, if you have 4 Mana points, and a Spell costs 1 Mana to use, you can cast it and you will be left with 3 Mana points. If you don't have enough Mana to use an Ability, you just can't use that Ability. Most Classes with Mana regenerate their Mana points to their Maximum at the end of an entire Adventure, so make good use of your Mana! It's scarce! We'll go through what an Adventure is later.
Mana.My Class Doesn't Have Mana!: Not all Classes use Mana. If your Class doesn't have Mana at all, then that's great! It's one less thing to be concerned about, and it means your Class makes up for it through more powerful Abilities.
Mana.<aside>If You're a Warlock...</aside>: Things change slightly if you're a Warlock. As it says in one of your Starting Abilities, your Mana points regenerate after each Combat, so use them all when fighting!
Mana.More About Mana:
Your Hero has a maximum number of Mana points depending on the Class. When you Level up, you might also gain +1 Max Mana. Other Abilities might give you more Max Mana.
The amount of Mana an Ability costs is represented by the  _blue flame_ icon and the number near it. Each Ability specifies individually how much Mana it costs.
You can keep track of your Mana by ticking the _magical circles_ on your paper Hero Sheet, or by using plastic tokens, or simply writing the number and erasing it. If you're using the Hero Creator online, there's a widget on your Hero Sheet to help you track your Mana.

Talents.Text: Talents are how you differentiate your Hero from any other Hero of the same Class. Talents are Abilities that come in the form of a choice: you may get to pick one out of a set of 2 to 6 possibilities. At Level 1, you usually get to pick from 2 or more (TODO) sets of Talents. All Classes get a Level 1 Utility Talent set and a Level 1 Class Talent set. This means that for each of these sets, pick one of the possible options. Add it to your Hero Sheet like you would any other Abilities you already have.
Talents.Rule of Thumb: Whenever you see Talent, it means it's a single choice out of a Talent set.
Talents.Level Up Talents: At each Level from 2 to 10, you will get another set of Talents, from which you can pick 1.
Talents.<aside>Can I Change Them?</aside>: Yes! Inbetween Adventures, you can completely change all your Talent options! If you don't feel like you made the right choices, you can just choose again!

Extra Talents (WIP).Text: We previously established you can ony have one Talent per Talent set. That's not entirely true, and there's a reason we've kept the use of the Intelligence Stat mysterious until now... You can get extra Talents equal to your Focus. Aside from the 1 free Talent you get per set, you can have an extra number of Talents equal to your Focus. For example, at Level 1, if your Focus is 2, you can have 3 Utility Talents and 1 Class Talents (1 free Utility Talent, 1 free Level 1 Class Talent, and 2 extra Utility Talents). Or you can have 2 Utility Talents and 2 Level 1 Class Talents. You're free to mix and match which Talents you get. At higher Levels, you can let go of extra Talents from lower levels for more powerful, higher Level Talents.
Extra Talents (WIP).<aside/>What is \"Keystone\"?</aside>: Some Talents have an orange glow and are listed as Keystone. As it says on every Keystone Talent, you can't have more than one Keystone Talent for that given Level. This is usually because those Talents are very powerful or contradict eachother.
Extra Talents (WIP).Almost Finished: You're almost done! Just a few little things to touch before you can take your Hero and play!

Equipment.Text: Every hero needs equipment, be it a sword, a robe, or a backpack full of adventuring gadgets and rations. When creating your Hero, you have a budget of 1000 {Gold}Gold to buy starting gear for your Hero. There are 3 things you should worry about when starting out: a weapon, a set of armor, and other useful items. The Weapons, Armors, and Shop & Prices chapters are one after another, on page TODO (and they each have a respective page on the website).
Equipment.<aside>Tracking your items and gold</asi:
You can take note of what items you have on your Hero Sheet.
You will need to keep acount of what you buy and how much {Gold}Gold you have left. After finishing shopping for items, any {Gold}Gold still left will carry on to your Hero.
Equipment.<aside>If you're doing it online</aside>:
If you're building your Hero with the Hero Creator online, switch to to the Shop section. Over there you can navigate between the Weapons, Armors, and Goods shops, each with separate categories for items.
Clicking Add on an item will add it to the cart. When you're done, hit the "Checkout" button, and all of the bought items will appear on your Hero Sheet automatically, and your {Gold} will be tracked as well.

Weapons.Text:
Head on over to the Weapons chapter on page TODO. You can find a list of all weapons in the game, so feel free to pick and choose within your budget. The cost of each weapon is represented by the little {Gold} icon and a number next to it.
Each weapon's Damage is different and is increased by certain Stats you have, most commonly Might and Instinct.
Weapons.Weapon Effects: All weapons in QuestGuard are different! Each weapon has a different Damage, Stats, and Range configuration, might require 1, 2 or 3 Action Points to attack, and 90% of them have an extra special effect, written in green text. This can be a Critical Strike, a passive effect, an extra Ability-like effect, and many more. Your hero is your canvas, and your weapon is the brush you will use to spill blood.
Weapons.<aside>Stat requirements</aside>: Some weapons have Stat requirements. For example, the Hand Axe requires you to have at least 1 Might and 1 Dexterity. If you don't, you can't use this weapon properly, and attacks with it will count as improvised attacks, which will deal just 1d4 + Might Damage, with no extra effects. For extra rules on this, see the Improvised Attack Ability on the Default Moves page.

Armors.Text: Next up is the Armors chapter on page TODO. Very similarly to the Weapons chapter, here you will find all armors in the game. They are split between categories, but any Hero can wear any 1 armor type (unless you're a Dwarf -- Dwarves can wear 2 armor sets). Protect yourself as you wish, and save some money for food, a backpack, and other useful items!
Armors.<aside>What about magic items?</aside>: The weapons and armors you've seen are regular ones, but you will be able to get most powerful ones later in the game, either buying them from special magic shops, or getting them as loot from monsters and dungeons!

Adventuring Gear.Text: Lastly, flip to the Shop & Prices page and you'll see whole pags of other small bits and pieces, like bedrolls, flasks, and whatever an explorer needs. You're going on an adventure, not just for slaying monsters, but you will most likely spend days out in the wilderness, have to cross crevices and mountainous terrain, disarm traps or set your own, and much more. Only a third of the game is commonly spent fighting; the rest is for exploring, roleplaying, and solving problems in-game. You'll need some quality items for that.
Adventuring Gear.<aside>Suggestions</aside>:
First, have enough food to last you a few days, at 5{Gold} per day's rations. If you need arrows, bolts, or gunpowder, do not forget to buy these. You can get a lifetime supply of these for 100{Gold} to 150{gold}.
To carry all these items, you'll be needing a 40{Gold} backpack, and probably 5 torches for the dark nights or closed caverns, worth 3{Gold} a piece.
The rest is up to you!

Good Luck.Text: You're done. Your Hero is ready to adventure on! Keep reading to see more important rules you should know about.

Other Abilities.Feats: There exist a set of entirely optional extra Abilities called Feats, which you can find at page TODO. Feats are extra ways to play your character: they might allow you to borrow power from other Classes or Races (multiracing/multiclassing), unlock unusual fighting techniques or playstyles, etc. You can get as many Feats as you want, but each Feat has its own cost, which most of the time require you to sacrifice some of your base Stats (e.g. -1 Might). You can get Feats inbetween Adventures. Note that Feats are permanent and can't be changed inbetween Adventures, but there are services which help remove Feats. On the Shop & Prices chapter on page TODO, you can find prices for all Services over there.
Other Abilities.Default Moves: Default Moves are a set of Abilities everyone always has access to. You don't need to put these on your Hero Sheet, unless they're important for you and feel like you should have them there.

Quirks.Text: At the end of every Adventure, the Quest Master gives each Hero a Quirk, positive or negative, based on how they fared during that Adventure. A Quirk is either a small phobia or physical or mental trauma (if it's negative), or the opposite if it's positive. Quirks will give small boosts (or debuffs) to Skills, sometimes Stats, or give (or take) Initiative in combats with certain creatures. For example, a Hero may receive Megalophobia, the fear of large creatures, and will have -1 Initiative in Combats against large creatures. The full list of Quirks can be found on page TODO, but should remain only for the eyes of the Quest Master for now. Let yourself be surprised by how your Hero changes throughout the campaigns.
Quirks.<aside>Quest Master's tips</aside>: A good Quest Master will seek to always keep each Hero in the balance, and not overwhelm them with good or bad Quirks; as a general rule of thumb, a Hero should have the same number of positive and negative Quirks. If a Hero receives a negative Quirk, the next one should be positive. Also, a good Quest Master will make sure to help and not impair their Heroes. If a Hero is based on Presence, the Quest Master should not decrease that Hero's Presence. The Quirks distributed to the Heroes should also be similar in power: it would be unfair to give a Hero +1 in a Stat, and give another +1 in a Skill. Alas, Quirks are earned. Act a certain way and get a Quirk to represent how you acted, and if the Quest Master wants to run a more gritty, difficult Adventure, it is up to them how they distribute the Quirks.

Combo.Text: You will likely see the word Combo on various Abilities. Some Abilities can apply a Combo, others can consume a Combo. When you apply a Combo, you apply it to the target of the attack or Ability. When someone else would hit the target with an attack or Ability that lists something like "Combo: +1d4 Damage", whatever is written there happens, and then the Combo is removed from the target.
